an3.39:1.1: Siddhattha’s reflections are, in the developed legend, said to be prompted by the divine messengers, whereas here they arise from spontaneous reflection. One of the reasons for this kind of narrative shift was the popularity in later times of narrative art depicting the events of the Buddha’s life. Pagodas and temples were lavishly illustrated with such scenes, and pilgrims would be taken around around them and the stories explained by teachers. Making the events dramatic and concrete allowed them to be shared more widely: how do you illustrate a thought?
an3.39:1.4: From this it would appear that the _nivāsana_ is comparable to what bhikkhus call _antarāvāsaka_, i.e. a robe for the lower body that is worn “inside the monastery”, i.e. a dhoti or sarong. | The turban—elaborate versions of which feature prominently in artwork—and jacket were banned for monastics as being too much like lay clothes ([pli-tv-kd8:29.1.1]()).
an3.39:1.5: As with Vipassī ([dn14:1.34.3]()). Parasols are allowed for monastics with restrictions ([pli-tv-bu-vb-sk57](), [pli-tv-bi-vb-pc84]()).
an3.39:2.2: Most of the types of musicians met in ancient India were men—wandering bards and the like. These women would have been courtesans sponsored by the state. Kauṭilya recommends that a Superintendent of Courtesans be appointed, who would sponsor the business and administer it with a detailed legal framework that provided both protection for the women as well as penalties. Brothels were run by madams who were retired courtesans. Workers were taxed at the rate of twice the fee of a sexual encounter each month. These taxes were then used to provide education in the fine arts: “singing; playing musical instruments; reciting; dancing; acting; writing; painting; playing the lute, ﬂute, and drum; reading another’s mind; preparing perfumes and garlands; conversation; shampooing; and the arts of a courtesan” (Arthaśāstra 2.17).
an3.39:2.3: _Bilaṅga_ is allowed with other medicinal fruits at [pli-tv-kd6:6.1.4](). It is Sanskrit _viḍaṅga_, identified as *embelia ribes* or “false black pepper”.
